questions.question: A worker crashes after completing two recorded activities in a long agent workflow. What should durable replay do?
options: Reuse logged results for completed activities and run the missing work
Ask the user to repeat every approval before resuming
Restart every activity so the sequence is repeated from scratch
Discard the workflow because model calls are nondeterministic
questions.explanation: Replay reruns deterministic workflow code but returns event-log outputs for completed activities, executing only unfinished work. Restarting all activities from scratch can repeat side effects and rebill completed LLM calls.

questions.question: Which part of durable execution must be deterministic so it can be replayed against the event log?
options: The result of a payment processor
The external LLM response
The orchestration workflow
The wall-clock latency of a tool
questions.explanation: The workflow defines branches and sequencing, so it must replay deterministically against the event log. The external LLM response is nondeterministic and belongs in a logged activity whose prior output is reused.

questions.question: What is an activity in the lesson's durable-execution model?
options: A human-readable summary of every model token
A non-deterministic operation whose inputs and outputs are logged
A permanent lock that prevents another worker from resuming
The deterministic code that chooses all workflow branches
questions.explanation: An activity is a potentially failing unit—such as an LLM call, file write, or API request—whose inputs and outputs are logged. The workflow is deterministic orchestration that sequences those activities.

questions.question: An approval arrives two days after the agent requested it. What feature lets the workflow resume at the waiting point?
options: A longer model context containing the old terminal log
An LLM retry that guesses whether the user approved
A fresh process that reconstructs the approval from memory
A durable human-input state stored with the checkpoint
questions.explanation: Persist the waiting-for-human state so an approval arriving later resumes from the same checkpoint after a restart. A longer prompt does not preserve process state, and guessing approval bypasses the user.

questions.question: A team has a short, read-only lookup that finishes in seconds and never waits for a person. What does the lesson say about durable execution?
options: It may be unnecessary for short read-only runs
It eliminates the need to bound tool calls
It is mandatory for every read-only request
It improves correctness by replaying model outputs deterministically
questions.explanation: For a seconds-long read-only lookup with no human wait or side effect, recovery benefits may not justify durable-execution overhead. The lesson lists such cases as poor fits, not mandatory use.

questions.question: A workflow places a wall-clock timestamp directly in an orchestration branch. Why can this break replay?
options: The event log automatically converts timestamps into model outputs
A timestamp makes every external activity idempotent
Replay skips deterministic workflow code and only runs tools
The same workflow state may take a different branch when replayed later
questions.explanation: A wall-clock timestamp can differ between the original run and replay, sending deterministic orchestration down a different branch. Idempotency prevents duplicate side effects but does not stabilize time; record nondeterministic effects or use a replay-stable clock API.
